content: The Guide for Establishing a Pathology Laboratory in the Context of Cancer Control is a comprehensive document published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2019. It provides detailed guidance for program managers and health officials on the minimum requirements for setting up and maintaining pathology laboratories, particularly those offering histopathology and cytopathology services. The guide emphasizes the critical role of pathology in cancer diagnosis, treatment, and management, and highlights the need for reliable and accessible pathology services to support national cancer control programs. The publication is licensed under Creative Commons, allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent terms. If the guide is translated, a disclaimer must be included stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guide underscores the global burden of cancer, which is the second leading cause of mortality worldwide, with an estimated 18 million new cases and 10 million deaths annually. By 2040, the incidence of cancer is projected to rise to 30 million cases per year. Effective cancer control requires pathology services for definitive diagnosis, which involves morphological and phenotypical examination of tissues and fluids. For solid tumors, histopathological parameters such as type, grade, and extent of cancer are essential for determining optimal treatment. Cytopathology is also widely used for cancer screening, diagnosis, and surveillance. Pathology and laboratory medicine (PALM) encompass a range of diagnostic testing that informs approximately 70% of all medical decisions. These services are vital for diagnosis, treatment guidance, prognosis, and monitoring outcomes. Despite their importance, access to pathology services is highly variable across the globe. While 95% of high-income countries report general availability of pathology services, only 26% of low-income countries have similar access. Many lowand middle-income countries face significant challenges, including under-resourced laboratories, lack of trained personnel, inadequate equipment, and unreliable diagnostic quality. The guide identifies key barriers to accessing pathology services, such as weak leadership and governance, insufficient infrastructure, lack of trained human resources, poor service delivery, inadequate health information systems, and limited financing. It also outlines the three phases of pathology services—pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical—each of which involves specific components of specimen management. The pre-analytical phase includes specimen collection, fixation, identification, and transportation, while the analytical phase involves tissue processing, staining, and examination. The post-analytical phase focuses on reviewing slides, reporting results, and archiving patient data. The guide aims to support the establishment of safe and high-quality pathology laboratories, tailored to local contexts and needs. It highlights the importance of pathology in achieving universal health coverage and addressing the rising global cancer burden. By improving access to essential pathology services, health systems can enhance timely diagnosis and effective treatment, ultimately reducing preventable cancer deaths.
